content: The GUSTO-I trial, formally known as the Global Utilization of Streptokinase and t-PA for Occluded Coronary Arteries-I Trial, was a large-scale, randomized clinical study involving 41,021 patients. These patients presented with acute myocardial infarction (AMI) and ST-segment elevation within six hours of symptom onset. The trial aimed to evaluate the efficacy of four different thrombolytic strategies. Importantly, there were no restrictions on enrollment based on age or the presence of cardiogenic shock. However, patients were excluded if they had a history of prior stroke, active or recent bleeding, recent trauma or major surgery, non-compressible vascular punctures, or prior treatment with streptokinase or anistreplase. The thrombolytic regimens included: 1. Streptokinase alone. 2. Accelerated t-PA (tissue plasminogen activator) administered as 1 mg/kg over one hour (up to a maximum of 90 mg, with 10% given as a bolus). 3. Streptokinase combined with subcutaneous heparin. 4. A combination of t-PA and streptokinase, administered simultaneously through separate cannulas, with the same intravenous heparin regimen. The primary endpoint of the trial was all-cause mortality at 30 days. Mortality data for inpatients were recorded on the main case report form, while post-discharge mortality data were collected via return postcards or telephone follow-up. Secondary endpoints included stroke, the composite of death or stroke, and the composite of death or nonfatal, disabling stroke. Neurological deficits that were fatal or persisted for at least 24 hours were reviewed by an independent, blinded committee. Stroke events were classified as primary intracranial hemorrhage, non-hemorrhagic infarction, hemorrhagic conversion of infarction, or unknown. Anatomical or diagnostic confirmation of stroke was obtained in 93% of cases. Bleeding complications were categorized as severe or life-threatening if they involved intracranial bleeding or caused hemodynamic compromise requiring intervention. Moderate bleeding was defined as bleeding that necessitated a blood transfusion. To analyze the relationship between baseline characteristics, clinical outcomes, and age, patients were arbitrarily divided into four age groups: <65 years, 65–74 years, 75–84 years, and ≥85 years. Discrete variables were summarized using frequencies and percentages, while continuous variables were described using means ± standard deviations or medians with interquartile ranges (25th and 75th percentiles). Clinical outcomes were tabulated by both age category and treatment assignment. Kaplan-Meier estimates were calculated for 24-hour, 30-day, and 1-year mortality to assess treatment effects across the different age groups. These age groups were chosen to facilitate visual inspection of trends in the data. Ordinary least-squares regression was employed to determine the statistical significance of relationships between age and baseline characteristics. Logistic regression was used to evaluate the statistical significance of the relationship between age and 30-day outcomes of interest. Cox proportional hazards modeling techniques were applied to assess the statistical significance of the relationship between 1-year mortality and age. For both types of mortality models, the shapes of the relationships were evaluated using cubic spline functions.
